questions.explanation: The linear bridge acts on the final feature dimension and preserves batch and patch-token axes.

questions.question: How does ToyVLM turn projected visual tokens into the input for its head?
options: It sorts tokens by pixel brightness and drops the batch axis
It mean-pools the patch tokens and applies the linear head
It decodes each token as a separate image
It replaces the projector with a convolution over text
questions.explanation: The demo averages projected patch features over the token axis before classifying the resulting vector.

questions.question: Concatenating three deep feature tensors of shape (4,16,32) along the last axis gives what shape?
questions.explanation: The batch and token dimensions stay fixed while the three 32-wide features form a 96-wide representation.

questions.question: When does the CMER-style check flag a visual token in the helper?
options: When similarity is above 0.25 and confidence is below 0.8
Whenever both values are exactly zero
Only when the token index is even
When similarity is below 0.25 and confidence is above 0.8
questions.explanation: The rule looks for a confident prediction whose visual-text agreement is unusually low.

questions.question: What problem does the projector solve in a vision-language model?
options: It maps visual feature width into the language model's expected width
It converts every image into a hard class ID
It removes the token sequence so text has no visual context
It normalizes only the optimizer learning rate
questions.explanation: The bridge aligns representations from the vision encoder with the dimensional interface consumed by the language side.

questions.question: Which loss matches the demo's integer class targets for the ToyVLM head?
options: Mean squared error between token positions
Cross-entropy over the logits
IoU between image masks
A triplet loss over bounding boxes
questions.explanation: The classifier produces logits for discrete classes, so cross-entropy is the matching supervised objective.
